Excel ToolKit ("XLTK") - Help

Introduction

Excel ToolKit ("XLTK") is a powerful library of functions that can be used in MS Excel to convert dates into strings for different languages. These strings are then easily used for display purposes. Users are reminded that these functions return strings and as such, they cannot be used for calculation purposes. Version 1.00 of XLTK converts date in Canadian and US English and Canadian French.

Each function requires one or more parameters and some accept optional parameters. Optional parameters can always be ommited in which case, default values are used.

Parameters are not case sensitive. For example "LOnG" is treated the same as "long", "lonG" or "LONG".

DateToText Function

Returns a string a date in a specific language and format.

Syntax: DateToText( xlDate, lang, fmtId, [yearLength], [isOrdinal], [isAll] )

Parameter Status Type Sample
xlDate Required Any valid Excel date expressed as a number A1=Today(), A1=2025/12/31, A1=December 31, 2025, etc. (2025/12/25 is 46022 fo instance.)
lang Required String Output language: "FR-CDN", "F" or "FR" for French, "EN-US", "EN" or "E" for English
fmtId Optional Integer Numeric value: 1 to 7 as per the table below where [YY]YY is controled by the yearLength parameter:
fmtId EN-US FR-CAN
1 Mmmm DD, [YY]YY -> December 31, [20]26 DD Mmmm [YY]YY -> 31 décembre [20]26
2 Mmm. DD, [YY]YY -> Dec. 31, [20]26 Mmm. DD, [YY]YY DD Mmm. YY(YY) -> 31 déc. [20]26
3 Mmm- DD-[YY]YY -> Dec-31-[20]26 DD-Mmm-[YY]YY -> 31-déc-[20]26
4 YYYY-MM-DD -> 2026-12-31 DD-MM-YYYY -> 31-12-2026
5 Mmmm [YY]YY -> December [20]26 mmmm [YY]YY -> Décembre [20]26
6 Weekday, Mmmm DD, [YY]YY -> Thursday, December 31, [20]26 Weekday, DD Mmmm [YY]YY -> Jeudi 31 décembre [20]26
7 Mmm-YYYY -> Dec-2026 Mmm-YYYY -> Déc-2026
yearLength Optional Integer 4 for YYYY and 2 for YY. If ommited or different than 4 or 2, 4 (YYYY) is applied
isOrd Optional Boolean TRUE or FALSE. Default is FALSE.
If TRUE, adds the proper ordinal suffix to the day: "1st", "2nd ", "3rd", "4th", etc. for English and "1er" for French
Applies to fmtId #1 only ('December 31st, 2025' or '1er décembre 2025' for instance)
isALL Optional Boolean TRUE or FALSE. Default is FALSE.
Applies if isOrd is TRUE and lang is "FR".
IF TRUE, adds ordinal suffix "e" for "2e", "3e", etc in French
Has no effect on English strings

Optional parameters

It is important to note that when an optional parameter is used, its position within the function parameters list must be maintained. For instance, if isOrd is used, a placeholder for yearLength must be present:
=DateToText(date, Lang, FormatID, isOrd, IsAll) --> Invalid as there is no parameter between FormatID and isOrd for yearLength
=DateToText(date, Lang, FormatID, ,isOrdinal, IsAll) --> Valid. The default for yearLength will be used since its value is 'empty'
=DateToText(date, Lang, ,isOrd, isAll) --> Invalid as there is one missing parameter between Lang and isOrdinal
=DateToText(date, Lang, , ,isOrd, IsAll) --> Valid. The default for FormatID and yearLength will be used
Example:
=DateToText(A1, A2,A3,A4,A5) where:
Cell(A1): 2025/12/25 (number 46022)
Cell(A2): "FR"
Cell(A3): 1.2 -> 1
Cell(A4): 4 (or is empty)
Cell(A5): TRUE (or is empty)
Cell(A6): FALSE (or is empty)
returns "December 25th, 2025"

getMonthNum Function

Returns an integer n from 1 to 12 representing the nth month of the year.

Syntax: getMonthNum(xlDate)

Parameter Status Type Sample
xlDate Required Any valid Excel date expressed as a number A1=Today(), A1=2025/12/31, A1=December 31, 2025, etc. (2025/12/25 is 46022 fo instance.)

This is the equivalent of Excel buit-in function Month().

Examples:
=getMonthNum(A1) where Cell(A1) contains 2025/12/25 (number 46022), returns 12 (December being the 12th month of the year)
=getMonthNum(46022) returns 12 (46022 being December 25, 2025 and December being the 12th month of the year)

getMonthName Function

Returns a string representing the translation of the month of a date in a specific language and format.

Syntax: getMonthName(xlDate, lang, [fmt])


Parameter Status Type Sample
xlDate Required Any valid Excel date expressed as a number A1=Today(), A1=2025/12/31, A1=December 31, 2025, etc. (2025/12/25 is 46022 fo instance.)
lang Required String Output language: "FR-CDN", "F" or "FR" for French, "EN-US", "EN" or "E" for English
fmt Optional String Output format: "Short" for abbreviated month, "Long" for full month name. Default is "Long"

Examples:
=getMonthName(A1, A2) where Cell(A1) contains 2025/12/25 (number 46022), Cell(A2) contains "FR-CDN" returns "Décembre"
=getMonthNum(46022, "FR-CDN", "Short") returns "Déc" (46022 being December 25, 2025)

getDayNum Function

Returns an integer n from 1 to 31 representing the nth day of the month of a specific date

Syntax: getDayNum(xlDate)

Parameter Status Type Sample
xlDate Required Any valid Excel date expressed as a number A1=Today(), A1=2025/12/31, A1=December 31, 2025, etc. (2025/12/25 is 46022 fo instance.)

This is the equivalent of Excel buit-in function Day().

Examples:
=getDayNum(A1) where Cell(A1) contains 2025/12/25 (number 46022), returns 25 (December 25 being the 25th day of the month)
=getMonthNum(46022) returns 25 (46022 being December 25, 2025 and December 25 being the 25th day of the month)

getDayName Function

Returns a string representing the translation of the weekday of a date in a specific language and format.

Syntax: getDayName(xlDate, lang)

Parameter Status Type Sample
xlDate Required Any valid Excel date expressed as a number A1=Today(), A1=2025/12/31, A1=December 31, 2025, etc. (2025/12/25 is 46022 fo instance.)
lang Required String Output language: "FR-CDN", "F" or "FR" for French, "EN-US", "EN" or "E" for English

Examples:
=getDayName(A1, A2) where Cell(A1) contains 2025/12/25 (number 46022), Cell(A2) contains "EN-US" returns "Thursday", December 25, 2025 being a Thursday
=getMonthNum(46022, "FR-CDN") returns "jeudi" (46022 being December 25, 2025 which is a Thursday or "jeudi" in French)

getYearName Function

Returns a string representing the year of a specific date

Syntax: getYearName(xlDate, yearLength)

Where:
Parameter Status Type Sample
xlDate Required Any valid Excel date expressed as a number A1=Today(), A1=2025/12/31, A1=December 31, 2025, etc. (2025/12/25 is 46022 fo instance.)
yearLength Optional Integer 4 for YYYY and 2 for YY. If ommited or different than 4 or 2, 4 (YYYY) is applied

This is the equivalent of Excel buit-in function TEXT(xlDate, "YYYY") for yearLength = 4 and TEXT(xlDate, "YY") for yearLength = 2.

Examples:
=getYearName(A1) where Cell(A1) contains 2025/12/25 (number 46022), returns "2025"
=getYearName(46022, 2) returns "25"

getOrdinal Function

Returns a string representing the ordinal of an integer. The string can be appended to any integer.

Syntax: getYearName(num, lang, isAll)

Parameter Status Type Sample
num Required Integer Any Integer
Passing a decimal number ( 2.5 for instance) will throw an error
lang Required String Output language: "FR-CDN", "F" or "FR" for French, "EN-US", "EN" or "E" for English
isAll Optional Boolean Applies to French only
If "TRUE", ordinal "e" is return for integers other than 1
Has no effect on English numbers

Examples:
=getOrdinal(A1, "FR") where Cell(A1) contains 1, returns "er" (can be appended to 1 to get "1er")
=getOrdinal(31, "en", TRUE) returns "st" (can be appended to 31 to get "31st"). Note that the third parameter isAll = "TRUE" has no effect on English ordinals
=getYearName(Day(46022), "en") returns "th" (46022 is December 25, 2025 and Day(46022) = 25 whose ordinl is "th". Can be appended to 25 to get "25th" )
=getOrdinal(6, "FR") returns "" (or empty) since the default value for isAll is "FALSE"
=getOrdinal(6, "FR", TRUE) returns "e" (can be appended to 6 to get "6e")

Note1: Function DateToText() uses getOrdinal() when the isOrd parameter of function DateToText() is set to TRUE. We have made this function available to provide users with the ability to append an ordinal string to any integer.

Note2: MS Excel does not allow a function to return a formated string. For that reason, it is not possible to return the ordinal in superscript (31st for instance). To work around this limitation, users can use the provided functions to create a series of strings that can be sent to MS Word for instance. In MS Word, users can format the ordinal mergefield to suprscript like this:

1. Define mailMerge field names: Cell(A1) = "mrgMonth" ; Cell(B1) = "mrgDay" ; Cell(C1) = "mrgOrd" ; Cell(D1) = "mrgYear"

2. Get the data: Cell(A2) = "=getMonthName(46022, "EN")" ; Cell(B2) = "getDayNum(46022)" ; Cell(C2) = "getOrdinal(B2)" ; Cell(D2) = "getYearName(46022)"

3. Results: Cell(A2) = "December" ; Cell(B2) = "25" ; Cell(C2) = "st" ; Cell(D2) = "2025"

4. In MS Word, use this: {MERGEFIELD mrgMonth} {MERGEFIELD mrgDay}{MERGEFIELD mrgOrd \*sup} {MERGEFIELD mrgYear} Result: December 25th, 2025.

This is very flexible and can be used in numerous maners. It prevents the use of complex formulas and coding in MS Word to get the ordinal in superscript.

You can build strings like "1er décembre 2025", "25e jour du mois de décembre", "21st day of september of '99", etc.

While XLTK returns French month and day names in lower cases, using the MS Word "\*Caps" switch, you can get "Février 2025" or "Lundi, 1er août 1954" for instance.
